edits.walkthrough_append: **Worked step:** time one swing like a scientist. First, pull the bob a small distance to one side and let it go. Next, count 'zero' as it passes the lowest point, then time ten full swings (each to-and-fro is one oscillation) and divide by ten to get the time period of a single swing. Then repeat with a longer thread — the period grows; repeat with a heavier bob — nothing changes. **In the exam:** the time period depends on the length of the pendulum, not on the bob's mass or the smallness of the swing. **Check yourself:** why does a grand-father clock's pendulum keep perfect time? Its length is fixed, so every swing takes exactly the same interval.

**Worked step:** trace one treasure from source to use. First, a forest: trees hold soil with their roots, drink in carbon dioxide, give out oxygen, shelter birds and yield timber and medicines — use it faster than it regrows and the slope beneath stands bare. Next, the soil: it took thousands of years to form from rock; one careless season of erosion can wash it away. Then a fossil fuel: coal buried for millions of years burns in minutes and cannot be remade. **In the exam:** classify each as renewable or non-renewable and give one conservation habit for each. **Check yourself:** why is soil renewable 'only slowly'? Rock weathers to soil over centuries, so for human lifetimes it must be treated as almost non-renewable.

**Worked step:** walk a plant from root to flower. First, the roots anchor and drink — water and minerals enter here. Next, the stem holds the plant up and runs the two-way transport: water up in the vessels, food down and around. Then the leaves cook — photosynthesis turns water, carbon dioxide and sunlight into food. Finally the flower does the reproduction, making pollen and, after pollination, seeds that grow into new plants. **In the exam:** match part to function in one line each — root: anchor and absorb; stem: support and transport; leaf: food factory; flower: reproduction. **Check yourself:** why can a plant live without its flowers for a season, but not without its roots? Because roots keep the water supply running; flowers only carry the next generation.

**Worked step:** price one ribbon like a shopkeeper. First read the rate: ₹15.50 per metre — one rupee and fifty paise, written with the point separating rupees from paise. Next, the length wanted is 3.25 m, so multiply 15.50 × 3.25, place the point so four decimal places return, and get ₹50.375, rounded to ₹50.38. Then check by rough estimate: 3 metres at about ₹15 is ₹45, and a bit more for the quarters — ₹50 is reasonable. **In the exam:** in money problems, keep the point as the rupee–paise wall; in measurement, line it up with the unit (m, cm). **Check yourself:** why does 0.75 m of ribbon cost less than 1 m? Because 0.75 is three-quarters of the unit — decimals measure the part between whole numbers.

**Worked step:** run the seven-point check on two mystery objects. First, a stone and a mango seedling side by side: the seedling grows — taller each week; the stone only wears down. Next, give both water: the seedling takes it in and stays firm; the stone ignores it. Then watch response — the seedling's shoot bends towards the window within days; the stone never answers. Finally, time: the seedling makes new leaves and, in years, seeds of its own; the stone does neither. **In the exam:** list the life processes — nutrition, growth, respiration, response, excretion, movement, reproduction — and show the object has them together. **Check yourself:** why is movement alone not proof of life? A bus moves, a cloud drifts — but they grow no parts, repair nothing, and reproduce never; the signs work as a set.

**Worked step:** build and read a simple sundial. First, fix a stick (the gnomon) upright in a sunny open space and mark the tip of its shadow first thing in the morning. Next, return every hour and mark the new shadow-tip; by evening the marks sweep a fan across the ground — the shadow moves as the Sun appears to move westward. Then number the marks and the dial can tell the hour again tomorrow. **In the exam:** the story is fixed stick, moving Sun, sweeping shadow — the Sun's apparent motion does the measuring. **Check yourself:** why does a sundial fail on a cloudy day? No sunlight means no shadow — the dial needs the Sun as its moving hand.

**Worked step:** keep a weather diary for one school week. First, choose a fixed time — say 8 a.m. — and read the day's temperature, cloud cover, wind direction and any rain in your own words and numbers. Next, write the entry the same way every day: date, then each observation on its line, so entries can be compared. Then, at week's end, read the column downwards: which days were coolest, did the wind swing, did the clouds bring the rain? **In the exam:** the method is record, repeat, pattern — same time, same fields, then compare. **Check yourself:** why must the reading time be fixed? Weather changes through the day; a 7 a.m. reading next to a 2 p.m. one would compare morning with afternoon, not day with day.

**Worked step:** trace the Revolt along its one road. First, the spark: at Meerut on 10 May 1857, sepoys punished for refusing greased cartridges break open the jail and march to Delhi. Next, the spread: the proclamation of the old Mughal emperor Bahadur Shah Zafar as leader gives the rising a symbol, and Kanpur, Lucknow, Jhansi and Bihar rise under Nana Saheb, Begum Hazrat Mahal, Rani Lakshmibhai and Kunwar Singh. Then the counter-wave: British reinforcements retake Delhi by September 1857, and by 1858 the revolt is crushed — but Company rule is replaced by direct Crown rule. **In the exam:** answer in the order spark, leader, spread, result. **Check yourself:** why did the revolt ultimately fail? It stayed regional, lacked unified command and modern arms — brave uprisings, but not one coordinated war.

**Worked step:** do one piece of science on your own kitchen. First, observe: iron vessels in the sink develop reddish patches. Next, question: why does the patch appear where water sits longest? Then hypothesise: water plus air (moisture) makes iron rust. Test: keep one nail dry, one in water, one in oiled air for a week and compare. Finally conclude: only the wet nail rusts — the hypothesis stands. **In the exam:** name the steps in order — observation, question, hypothesis, experiment, conclusion — and match each sentence of a story to its step. **Check yourself:** what makes this method scientific? The test can be repeated by anyone, and the conclusion changes if the evidence does.

**Worked step:** meet your own image with a rule-book. First, stand a metre before a plane mirror: your image stands a metre behind the glass — distances on the two sides are equal. Next, raise your right hand: the image raises the hand on its right — which is your left, because left and right have swapped (lateral inversion). Then compare sizes: image and object match exactly, head up, feet down — upright and same size. Finally, try to touch it: your hand meets glass, not the image, because no light comes from behind — the image is virtual. **In the exam:** the four words that answer any plane-mirror question: same distance, same size, upright, laterally inverted — and virtual. **Check yourself:** why does the ambulance word look strange in a mirror? It is printed in reverse so that it reads correctly in drivers' mirrors — lateral inversion, used on purpose.

**Worked step:** read a torch like a cell diagram. First, the cell's two terminals: the metal cap is positive, the flat metal base negative — chemical paste inside separates their charges. Next, connect bulb, switch and cell in one loop; the moment the switch closes, chemical energy inside converts to electrical energy and the filament lights. Then try the cell the other way round — the torch still works, because a simple circuit only needs the push (voltage), not a direction. **In the exam:** name the conversion — chemical to electrical — and remember the pairing: one cell alone is a cell; two or more joined make a battery. **Check yourself:** why does a torch dim as its cells age? The chemical store inside is running down, so it can push less current for less time.

**Worked step:** follow a glucose molecule through its engine. First, digestion hands the bloodstream a simple sugar from the bread you ate. Next, breathing has loaded the blood with oxygen; both arrive at a muscle cell. Then, inside, the cell burns the sugar with that oxygen — glucose + oxygen give carbon dioxide, water and energy — and packs the energy into ATP, the cell's spendable fuel. The muscle contracts on it; the leftovers leave as every breath out. **In the exam:** the three-word frame is fuel, oxygen, energy — with carbon dioxide and water as the outputs. **Check yourself:** why do you pant after running upstairs? The muscles burned fuel faster than oxygen arrived, so the body repays the oxygen debt with deeper, faster breathing.

**Worked step:** test two cut-outs for congruence like a detective. First, check the type: two triangles, matching labels A↔P, B↔Q, C↔R. Next, measure the sides — AB = PQ, BC = QR, CA = RP: all three pairs equal. Then measure the angles — ∠A = ∠P, ∠B = ∠Q, ∠C = ∠R — all equal too. Finally, superpose: place one over the other and every edge and corner lies exactly on its partner. **In the exam:** the verdict phrase is same shape and same size — and when one figure must sit exactly on the other, write the correspondence in matching order. **Check yourself:** why does 'same shape' alone not prove congruence? Two photographs of different sizes share shape — size equality is the second half of the test.

edits.definition: Slow natural changes are transformations that unfold over years, centuries or longer — rock weathering into soil, rivers and wind eroding mountains grain by grain, iron rusting in damp air, the gradual wearing of old monuments. They are hard to notice while they happen, because no single day shows a difference, yet they are genuine changes: new substances form (rust from iron, soil from rock) and the original material never returns. What distinguishes them from fast changes like burning is only the timescale — the chemistry of change is the same, drawn out across ages.

Democracy is the system of government in which the people hold the power and exercise it by electing representatives who make laws and run the country on their behalf — the word itself comes from the Greek demos (people) and kratos (rule). Its pillars are regular free and fair elections in which every adult votes; the accountability of rulers, who hold office only as long as the voters' confidence lasts; the freedom to speak, question and organise; and the equality of every vote. Government by the people also means answering to the people — between elections as well as on polling day.

Government services are the essential facilities the state provides — or supervises — so that daily life is safe, healthy and workable for everyone: roads and public transport that move people and goods; schools and hospitals that build citizens and care for the sick; water supply, sanitation and electricity that no household can secure alone; police, courts and fire services that protect life and property; and welfare schemes for those who cannot yet help themselves. They are funded from public taxes and meant to reach every citizen — which is why their quality is the first test of how well a government governs.

Geographical diversity is the variety of physical features — mountains, plains, deserts, plateaus, coasts and forests — that nature packs into one country's borders. India holds them all within a single map: the freezing Himalayan wall in the north, the fertile Gangetic plain below it, the Thar desert in the west, the ancient Deccan plateau in the centre and south, and a long tropical coastline fringed by palms. That variety of land brings variety of climate, rivers, crops, wildlife and ways of living — diversity not as decoration but as the physical foundation of the country's richness.
